title: The unfortunate weathercock
sentences: Some men fortune carries in the palm of her hand, while for others she keeps her palm open only to box their ears with it.
We know of a case which will show before us a living example of fortune's caprice for both species alike.
We shall tell it as we heard it, not adding a single word.
…Thus around mid-December 1848 every man already rather longed for war,
and here in Pest in particular peace was very much out of fashion.
At the Nagypipa the guests made a terrible racket over their mugs of beer.
Declarations of war were circulating; the European war was being prepared.
At but one table sat two men in silence, to whom very aptly applied what the German says:
„Der eine schweigt, der andere hört zu.”
For the one did indeed seem to be pondering with the greatest attention
why the other kept silent, and meanwhile never took his questioning eyes off him.
This attentive man was none other than the humane Master János, of whom, if we tell you
that even in Metternich's day he had been sergeant-at-arms and deputy beadle to noble Pest, and yet with Metternich's fall did not lose his office,
as usually happens to the adherents of fallen ministries, we straightway make it guessable that he, whom we have marked out as fortune's chosen prototype, will surely be our man.
And if we tell you that the man at whom he cast such suspicious glances was a locksmith journeyman who had arrived from Vienna but yesterday, everyone may foretell from that as well
that fortune must persecute this one sorely, not merely because Master János casts suspicious glances at him,
but above all because he came to Hungary as a locksmith, where that cunning craft is practised wholesale at every village edge by the Vlach Gypsies.
Master János had indeed not read Lavater, yet from old tact he straightway read in the man's face
that this fellow must surely be brooding over some counter-revolutionary plot.
He edged closer to him.
– Whence come you, sir?
– he asked the stranger with a cunning look.
– Hjaj…
From Vienna – sighed the other, gazing at the bottom of his mug.
– What news there?
– Hjaj…
Nothing good.
– How so?
Nothing good?
What ails them, then?
– Hjaj…
They are terribly afraid of war.
– Afraid?
The impudence!
How dare they be afraid?
– Hjaj…
Sir, from thirty miles off I am not afraid of it either, but once I listened from a cellar
while they cannonaded in the street, and I found nothing beautiful in it.
Master János always found fresh grounds for suspicion.
He had a thought: he would ply the man with drink; perhaps thus he might come on the trail of some dangerous plot.
What does a locksmith's stomach need to get drunk?
At the second mug of beer his head already fell back, and he could scarcely move his tongue.
– Now for it!
– thought Master János.
– „Long live liberty!”
– he cried, raising his glass and waiting for the locksmith to clink his own against it.
The man did not keep him waiting long, and so far as his faltering tongue allowed, he echoed the cheer.
– There now, drink to someone – the deputy beadle coaxed his cunningly chosen victim.
– God knows, I am accustomed to drink only for myself.
– Do not jest, sir!
But drink to whoever you hold the greatest man upon earth!
– Upon the whole earth?
– asked the locksmith, reflecting that the whole earth is indeed uncommonly large, but of it he knows precious little.
– Yes, upon the whole earth!
Upon the whole round world – Master János affirmed.
The locksmith pondered, scratched his nose, scratched his ear, scratched his whole head,
and at last what came of it was: „long live Master Slimák!”
The deputy beadle was horrified at this declaration.
It was plain to him that this Master Slimák must surely be the chief of some gunpowder conspiracy.
And with that – without more ado – he seized the innocent locksmith by the collar and brevi manu escorted him to the town hall.
There he led him into some room and set the innocent man on his feet before a fat red-faced gentleman.
– This man is suspicious – he said to that fat red gentleman.
– First, he is audacious enough to fear war; second, impudent enough to sit from seven o'clock till nearly ten in one place without
speaking a word; and finally godless enough to drink a public toast to the health of a certain Master Slimák, who must be some suspicious person.
– Who is this Master Slimák?
– asked that fat red gentleman sternly.
– Nobody at all, sir – answered the trembling locksmith –, only my former master, a humane locksmith,
with whom I served four years; I should still be with him had his wife not beaten me away.
– That cannot be – answered the fat red gentleman.
– One does not commonly raise one's glass publicly for such persons.
– But I do not know what the custom is here.
– If you wished to drink, why did you not drink thus: long live constitutional liberty!
long live the Upper- and Lower-Danube armies, long live the publicity guaranteed by freedom of the press?
and more of the same sort.
– Hjaj sir, I could not learn all that in a month.
– But in three, I believe, you may learn it.
Master János, take this man under your protection.
The humane Master János therefore took the convicted delinquent by the collar, uti supra, and bore him to the appropriate cold lodging,
where he would have ample leisure to reflect on how he had come there.
The three months passed; it was already mid-March.
The humane Master János punctually released the locksmith who had served out his sentence, that he might prove how much his sentiments had improved through discipline,
and that he might stand in better opinion before Master János too, he expressed himself in solemn, indeed painfully solemn, tones thus:
– Long live liberty, long live the Hungarian soldiers!
Master János, at these words, fell back against the wall in horror.
First against the wall, but then several times against the locksmith's honoured collar,
and before the latter could recover from his fright, he was already with him again in the narrow room.
Instead of the fat red gentleman there was now a lean black-haired gentleman present, who, as soon as he understood the delinquent's transgression,
did not allow him to get a word in, but scolded him from head to foot and made it known to him
that if he wished his lot not to be worse hereafter, next time he must cry: „Long live the imperial army!
long live the granted constitution!
Long live one and strong Austria!”
This time he might escape worse consequences with a three months' imprisonment.
The locksmith, therefore, before he had taken three steps from his prison door, was led back again and sat out another respectable three months.
The three months passed once more.
It was then, I know not which day of June.
The humane Master János released his captive.
The wretched fellow even at the prison door began to declaim the phrases he had learned by way of conciliation:
– Long live Prince Windisch-Grätz!
Long live glorious Austria!
Master János only watched to see with what sort of weapon he would seize the irreclaimable man.
– Was it not enough that they locked you up twice?
You still do not know what you ought to say?
Come along!
And he bore him a third time into the narrow room.
Instead of the lean black gentleman, the fat red gentleman now examined him again.
– Obstinate man!
– he thundered at him, comprehending the magnitude of his offence.
– Do you know that for what you let escape your lips, had I not now sufficient mercy,
I might on my own responsibility have you locked up for another three months, but hand you over to the court martial: you would be quartered!!!!
The man was forced to rejoice at the further three-month imprisonment, so terrified was he.
– But after all, what ought I to have said?
– You ought to have said: „long live the republic, long live democracy, long live the revolution!”
The man had the cheers repeated to him once more and promised
that he would learn them, and with full resignation let himself be shut away again into the kingdom of darkness.
In the three months that followed, much changed, but not Master János's fortune;
no misfortune could drive him from his office, as it did so countless others; he was still deputy beadle, as of old.
Fortune bore him in the palm of her hand.
September had come.
The locksmith's time was up.
Master János summoned him from the prison.
From afar one could see on the prisoner's face that he now meant to say something very clever,
he took Master János's hand and, melted to tears, began his speech thus:
– Tell that gentleman inside, Master János, that I kiss his hands with humility,
and wish him from my pure heart: „long live the ribillion!”
Like a mad wolf upon a lamb, Master János seized the locksmith round the waist at this word,
and long it was before he recovered himself enough that, when he had set him down in the narrow room, he could put the nature of his wrath into words.
In the room, instead of the red fat gentleman, the lean black gentleman was once again present.
Master János stated the charge, and his outrage was great when the lean gentleman, instead of
as would have been proper, having the audacious man broken on the wheel, merely ordered him back to his prison for another three months.
On the third of November those condemned for lesser political offences were set free, among them the locksmith too.
When Master János opened the door for him, the man bound his mouth with his handkerchief and marched past him,
and by pantomime alone made known to the humane deputy beadle that henceforth he would keep his cheers to himself.
Yet let it be a consolation that he is not the only one in the world who cried out at the wrong season.
